lessons.title: Counting 1–10
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Count objects from 1 to 10
Write numerals 1–10
Match numbers to quantities
lessons.reading_material:
Numbers are all around us! When you count apples in a basket or steps up the stairs, you use numbers. The numbers 1 to 10 are the building blocks of all mathematics. Let's learn them together! Each number represents a specific quantity: 1 is one object, 2 is two objects, and so on up to 10.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Math is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. Counting 1–10 is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Count objects from 1 to 10; Write numerals 1–10; Match numbers to quantities. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: numeral, count, quantity, one-to-one correspondence. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Count classroom objects (books, pencils, chairs); Play the 'how many fingers' game. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

For homework, Count 5 different objects at home and draw them in your book. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review this lesson before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

Read it again, try the practice activity, and check yourself against the learning goals above; understanding usually arrives on the second or third pass, not the first.

lessons.title: My Local Area
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Identify features of a local area
Draw a simple map of the classroom/school
lessons.reading_material:
Geography is the study of places and people. Your local area includes homes, roads, parks, and shops. Maps help us understand where things are. A key (legend) shows what map symbols mean.

It's worth pausing to ask why My Local Area is part of the Geography curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. My Local Area is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Geography start to make a lot more sense.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to do a few specific things: Identify features of a local area; Draw a simple map of the classroom/school. Keep these goals in mind as you read -- they're not just a checklist for the teacher, they're a way for you to test yourself afterwards and see whether the lesson has really sunk in.

The key words to know for this lesson are: map, key, symbol, local area, direction, north. New topics often come with new vocabulary, and in Geography the vocabulary usually isn't just decoration -- each of these words points to a specific idea that you'll need again in later lessons, so it's worth being able to explain each one in your own words, not just recognise it when you see it.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

A good way to practise this lesson is: Draw a map of the classroom; Walk around the school and note features. Doing something hands-on with an idea -- rather than only reading about it -- is one of the fastest ways to make it stick, because your brain remembers things you've actually done far better than things you've only read.

For homework, Draw a simple map of your route to school. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review this lesson before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

To wrap up: My Local Area is one small piece of Geography, but it's a piece worth knowing solidly, because later lessons will lean on it without stopping to re-explain it. Take your time with it now, ask questions if anything feels unclear, and come back to reread this lesson whenever a later topic reminds you of it -- that kind of revisiting is exactly how real understanding builds up over a school year.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Geography is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. My Local Area is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Before getting into the details, think about where My Local Area shows up outside of the classroom. Ideas in Geography are rarely just for tests -- they usually connect to things you notice in everyday life, and part of getting good at Geography is training yourself to spot those connections instead of treating school topics as separate from the rest of the world.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

lessons.title: My Family History
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Describe how history is about the past
Create a simple family timeline
lessons.reading_material:
History is the study of the past. Your family has a history — stories of grandparents, parents, and you. A timeline shows events in the order they happened. We learn about the past from photos, stories, and objects.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning World History is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. My Family History is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Describe how history is about the past; Create a simple family timeline. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: past, present, future, timeline, history, memory. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'

Try this to reinforce what you just learned: Make a personal timeline from birth to now; Interview a grandparent about their childhood. It only takes a few minutes, but actively doing something with the idea works much better for memory than simply rereading the lesson a second time.

For homework, Draw a timeline of your life from birth to age 7. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Starry Night
info_cards.fact: "The Starry Night" by Vincent van Gogh. Painted in 1889, it shows a swirling night sky over a quiet village.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Sunflowers
info_cards.fact: "Sunflowers" by Vincent van Gogh. Van Gogh painted several versions of sunflowers in a vase using bright yellow paint.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Girl with a Pearl Earring
info_cards.fact: "Girl with a Pearl Earring" by Johannes Vermeer. A 17th-century Dutch portrait nicknamed the 'Mona Lisa of the North'.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
info_cards.fact: "The Great Wave off Kanagawa" by Katsushika Hokusai. A famous Japanese woodblock print showing a huge wave near Mount Fuji.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Hay Wain
info_cards.fact: "The Hay Wain" by John Constable. An English countryside scene showing a horse-drawn cart crossing a river.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Night Watch
info_cards.fact: "The Night Watch" by Rembrandt. A large group portrait of a militia company, known for its dramatic light and shadow.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Persistence of Memory
info_cards.fact: "The Persistence of Memory" by Salvador Dali. A surrealist painting famous for its melting clocks in a desert landscape.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Scream
info_cards.fact: "The Scream" by Edvard Munch. A Norwegian painting showing a figure with an agonized expression against a swirling sky.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Water Lilies
info_cards.fact: "Water Lilies" by Claude Monet. Part of a series of about 250 paintings Monet made of his garden pond in Giverny, France.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Christ the Redeemer
info_cards.fact: "Christ the Redeemer" by Paul Landowski. A giant statue overlooking Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, completed in 1931.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Mount Rushmore
info_cards.fact: "Mount Rushmore" by Gutzon Borglum. Carved into a mountain in South Dakota, it shows the faces of four U.S. presidents.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Statue of Liberty
info_cards.fact: "Statue of Liberty" by Frederic Auguste Bartholdi. A gift from France to the United States, standing in New York Harbor since 1886.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Great Sphinx of Giza
info_cards.fact: "The Great Sphinx of Giza" by Ancient Egyptian sculptors. A huge limestone statue with a lion's body and a human head, built thousands of years ago.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Lincoln Memorial statue
info_cards.fact: "The Lincoln Memorial statue" by Daniel Chester French. A large seated statue of President Abraham Lincoln in Washington, D.C.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Moai of Easter Island
info_cards.fact: "The Moai of Easter Island" by Rapa Nui people. Hundreds of giant stone head statues carved centuries ago on a remote Pacific island.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Terracotta Army
info_cards.fact: "The Terracotta Army" by Craftsmen of Qin Shi Huang. Thousands of life-sized clay soldier statues buried to guard an ancient Chinese emperor's tomb.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Winged Victory of Samothrace
info_cards.fact: "Winged Victory of Samothrace" by Unknown ancient Greek sculptor. An ancient marble statue of the goddess Nike, now in the Louvre Museum.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Little Mermaid (Copenhagen)
info_cards.fact: "The Little Mermaid (Copenhagen)" by Edvard Eriksen. A bronze statue sitting on a rock in Copenhagen's harbour, inspired by Hans Christian Andersen's tale.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Manneken Pis
info_cards.fact: "Manneken Pis" by Jerome Duquesnoy. A small, famous bronze fountain statue of a boy in Brussels, Belgium.

lessons.title: Colours and Shapes
lessons.subject: Art
learning_objectives: Name primary and secondary colours
Create art using basic shapes
lessons.reading_material:
The primary colours are red, yellow, and blue. Mix two primary colours to make secondary colours: red+yellow=orange, yellow+blue=green, blue+red=purple. Shapes: circle, square, triangle, rectangle. Artists use colour and shape to create pictures.

Here's a simple way to think about why this lesson matters. Learning Art is a bit like building with blocks -- each new idea rests on the ideas that came before it. Colours and Shapes is one of the blocks near the bottom of this particular tower, which is exactly why it's worth taking the time to understand it properly now rather than rushing past it.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to do a few specific things: Name primary and secondary colours; Create art using basic shapes. Keep these goals in mind as you read -- they're not just a checklist for the teacher, they're a way for you to test yourself afterwards and see whether the lesson has really sunk in.

The key words to know for this lesson are: primary colour, secondary colour, shape, circle, square, triangle. New topics often come with new vocabulary, and in Art the vocabulary usually isn't just decoration -- each of these words points to a specific idea that you'll need again in later lessons, so it's worth being able to explain each one in your own words, not just recognise it when you see it.

One thing that trips learners up with topics like this is going too fast: skimming the words without picturing what they actually mean. If a sentence in this lesson feels confusing, try slowing down and picturing a real example in your head, or drawing a quick sketch -- turning words into a picture is one of the best ways to catch a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit.

A good way to practise this lesson is: Colour mixing experiment with paint; Create a picture using only circles, squares, and triangles. Doing something hands-on with an idea -- rather than only reading about it -- is one of the fastest ways to make it stick, because your brain remembers things you've actually done far better than things you've only read.

For homework, Paint a rainbow using what you know about colours. This isn't just busywork -- it's a chance to use today's lesson somewhere outside the lesson itself, which is exactly how you'll know whether you really understood it or only thought you did.

When it's time to revise this topic before a test, remember: Review this lesson before the next class. A quick way to check yourself is to try explaining the whole lesson out loud in under a minute, as if you were teaching it to a younger student -- if you can do that smoothly, you're ready.

To wrap up: Colours and Shapes is one small piece of Art, but it's a piece worth knowing solidly, because later lessons will lean on it without stopping to re-explain it. Take your time with it now, ask questions if anything feels unclear, and come back to reread this lesson whenever a later topic reminds you of it -- that kind of revisiting is exactly how real understanding builds up over a school year.

info_cards.title: Did You Know?
info_cards.fact: A group of lions is called a pride.

info_cards.title: Did You Know?
info_cards.fact: Honey never spoils if it's stored properly.

info_cards.title: Famous Places
info_cards.fact: The Eiffel Tower in Paris, France was built in 1889 and is made almost entirely of iron.

info_cards.title: Philosophical Quote
info_cards.fact: "Well begun is half done." — Aristotle, ancient Greek philosopher.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "Be yourself; everyone else is already taken." — Oscar Wilde, Irish writer.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Marie Curie
info_cards.fact: Marie Curie was a scientist who discovered the elements polonium and radium, and won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: Silent Spring
info_cards.fact: "Silent Spring" by Rachel Carson (1962) is a non-fiction book that warned about the harm pesticides like DDT cause to birds and the environment, helping start the modern environmental movement.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: Cosmos
info_cards.fact: "Cosmos" by Carl Sagan explores the universe, the history of science, and our place among the stars.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Helen Keller
info_cards.fact: "Alone we can do so little; together we can do so much." — American author and disability-rights advocate who, though deaf and blind from infancy, learned to read, write, and speak.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Martin Luther King Jr.
info_cards.fact: "I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character." — American minister and civil-rights leader who led the 1963 March on Washington.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Rosa Parks
info_cards.fact: "I would like to be remembered as a person who wanted to be free... so other people would also be free." — American civil-rights activist whose refusal to give up her bus seat in 1955 helped spark the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Mahatma Gandhi
info_cards.fact: "Be the change that you wish to see in the world." — Indian lawyer and independence leader who led India's nonviolent struggle for freedom from British rule.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Walt Disney
info_cards.fact: "If you can dream it, you can do it." — American animator and entrepreneur who created Mickey Mouse and founded the Walt Disney Company.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Wilbur Wright
info_cards.fact: "It is possible to fly without motors, but not without knowledge and skill." — American inventor who, with his brother Orville, built and flew the first successful powered airplane in 1903.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Orville Wright
info_cards.fact: "The desire to fly is an idea handed down to us by our ancestors." — American inventor who, with his brother Wilbur, achieved the first powered, controlled airplane flight in 1903.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Mother Teresa
info_cards.fact: "Spread love everywhere you go." — Catholic nun and missionary who founded the Missionaries of Charity to help the poor and sick in Kolkata, India.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Florence Nightingale
info_cards.fact: "I attribute my success to this: I never gave or took an excuse." — British nurse known as the founder of modern nursing for her work improving hospital care during the Crimean War.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jane Goodall
info_cards.fact: "What you do makes a difference, and you have to decide what kind of difference you want to make." — British primatologist famous for her decades of research on wild chimpanzees in Tanzania.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Neil Armstrong
info_cards.fact: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." — American astronaut who became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Amelia Earhart
info_cards.fact: "The most effective way to do it is to do it." — American aviator who became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Fred Rogers
info_cards.fact: "There are three ways to ultimate success: the first way is to be kind, the second way is to be kind, the third way is to be kind." — American television host who created and hosted the children's show Mister Rogers' Neighborhood.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Maya Angelou
info_cards.fact: "Try to be a rainbow in someone's cloud." — American poet and author best known for her memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jim Henson
info_cards.fact: "Kids don't remember what you try to teach them. They remember what you are." — American puppeteer who created the Muppets, including Kermit the Frog and Sesame Street's characters.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Dr. Seuss (Theodor Geisel)
info_cards.fact: "Oh, the places you'll go!" — American children's author and illustrator who wrote The Cat in the Hat and Green Eggs and Ham.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Jacques Cousteau
info_cards.fact: "The sea, once it casts its spell, holds one in its net of wonder forever." — French explorer and filmmaker who pioneered ocean exploration and underwater documentary filmmaking.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Anne Sullivan
info_cards.fact: "Knowledge is love and light and vision." — American teacher best known for educating Helen Keller, who was both deaf and blind.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Louis Braille
info_cards.fact: "Access to communication in the widest sense is access to knowledge." — French educator who, blind himself from childhood, invented the Braille reading and writing system for the blind.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Benjamin Franklin
info_cards.fact: "An investment in knowledge pays the best interest." — American statesman, inventor, and writer who helped draft the U.S. Declaration of Independence.

lessons.reading_material:

A community is the group of people who live near each other and share places like schools, parks, and shops. lessons.title: Movement and Body Awareness
lessons.subject: Physical Education & Self-Defense
learning_objectives: Demonstrate basic locomotor skills
Identify major body parts used in movement
lessons.reading_material:
Our bodies can move in many ways: walk, run, jump, hop, skip, gallop. Physical activity is good for our heart, muscles, and mind. We should move our bodies every day. Always warm up before exercise and cool down after.

It's worth pausing to ask why Movement and Body Awareness is part of the Physical Education & Self-Defense curriculum at all. Every topic you study at school is chosen because it either explains something about the world you can see for yourself, or because it builds a mental tool you will keep using in more advanced lessons later. Movement and Body Awareness is one of those building-block topics: once you understand it well, several things that used to feel confusing in Physical Education & Self-Defense start to make a lot more sense.

Here is what success looks like for this lesson: Demonstrate basic locomotor skills; Identify major body parts used in movement. If you can honestly say you can do all of these by the time you finish, you've learned the lesson properly, not just skimmed it.

Some important terms appear in this lesson: locomotor, balance, coordination, warm-up, cool-down, heart rate. Try this trick: after reading through the lesson once, cover the page and see if you can explain each of these words to yourself (or better, to someone else) without peeking. If you get stuck on one, that's exactly the word to go back and reread about.

A common mistake with lessons like this one is memorising a fact without understanding why it's true. Memorised facts fade quickly and don't help when a question is asked in a slightly different way. Understanding, on the other hand, sticks around and lets you handle questions you've never seen before -- so whenever you can, ask yourself 'why is that true?' rather than just 'what is the answer?'
